title: Ninety-seven years, 31 moments
lede: From the Wollaston soda fountain to the lease sign in Lake George. Filter by thread. Where only the year is known, only the year is given.

events.title: The Wollaston store
events.text: Howard Deering Johnson buys a small store in Quincy’s Wollaston neighbourhood for $500 of borrowed money and takes on its debts. He rebuilds the soda fountain around a high-butterfat ice cream.

events.title: $240,000 of ice cream
events.text: Gross ice cream sales reach $240,000 a year.

events.title: First restaurant
events.text: Opens in Quincy, with fried clams and broiled swordfish as specialties. The Associated Press dates the first restaurant a year earlier.

events.title: First franchise
events.text: A restaurant in Orleans, on Cape Cod, sells Johnson’s food under his name. The operator pays for the building.

events.title: Out of Massachusetts
events.text: The first location outside the state opens in Milford, Connecticut.

events.title: 107 restaurants
events.text: Gross receipts are $10.5M and profit is $207,000.

events.title: The Pennsylvania Turnpike
events.text: The company wins the contract for 24 restaurants on the new turnpike. It keeps the monopoly until 1979.

events.title: Twelve left
events.text: Gasoline rationing cuts the chain from about 200 restaurants to 12. The company runs war-plant cafeterias to survive.

events.title: Lake George opens
events.text: Carl DeSantis opens a franchised restaurant on Route 9 in Lake George, New York. It will be the last one.

events.title: About 400 restaurants, and the first motor lodge
events.text: The chain is in 32 states. About 10% of units are company-owned turnpike sites. The company enters the motel business.

events.title: Lake Placid opens
events.text: The restaurant that Ron Butler would later own opens in Lake Placid, New York.

events.title: The son takes over
events.text: Howard Brennan Johnson, 26, becomes president. A restaurant opens in Times Square at Broadway and 46th Street.

events.title: Franey and Pépin
events.text: The company hires Pierre Franey and Jacques Pépin from Le Pavillon to oversee its commissary cooking. Pépin dates his own arrival to the spring of 1960.

events.title: Goes public
events.text: Howard Johnson Co. lists with 605 restaurants, 10 Red Coach Grills and 88 franchised motor lodges. 1960 net sales were $95M.

events.title: Company-owned outnumber franchised
events.text: For the first time the company runs more Howard Johnson’s than its licensees do.

events.title: Bangor opens
events.text: A restaurant and lounge opens beside the motor lodge on Odlin Road in Bangor, Maine.

events.title: Ground Round
events.text: The company starts a pub-style suburban chain.

events.title: The founder dies
events.text: Howard Deering Johnson dies. He had stayed on as chairman and treasurer until 1964.

events.title: Expansion stops
events.text: After the oil embargo, Howard B. Johnson halts new building. Highway sites produce 85% of the business.

events.title: 929 restaurants
events.text: 649 are company-operated. There are also 536 motor lodges, 32 Red Coach Grills and 63 Ground Rounds.

events.title: Imperial Group bids $630M
events.text: The British conglomerate offers $28 a share for 1,040 restaurants and 520 motor lodges. Howard B. Johnson collects $35.2M for his shares. Imperial owns the company from 1980.

events.title: Johnson leaves
events.text: Howard B. Johnson resigns as chairman, president and chief executive at the end of the year. G. Michael Hostage, a Marriott veteran, succeeds him.

events.title: Sold to Marriott and split
events.text: Marriott buys the company for $314M, keeps 418 company restaurants and sells the name, the lodges and 199 franchised restaurants to Prime Motor Inns for $235M. Imperial keeps Ground Round.

events.title: Franchise Associates Inc.
events.text: The restaurant franchisees incorporate their own company and receive an exclusive license to the Howard Johnson’s name for restaurants and signature foods.

events.title: Prime sells the hotel brand
events.text: Prime Motor Inns sells the Howard Johnson and Ramada franchise systems to an affiliate of Blackstone, and files for Chapter 11 in September.

events.title: About 160 left
events.text: About 110 franchised restaurants remain, and Marriott has 50. Franchise Associates buys 17 of Marriott’s.

events.title: Eight left; Times Square closes
events.text: The Associated Press counts eight restaurants in May. The Times Square restaurant closes that year.

events.title: Three left
events.text: Waterbury, Connecticut leaves the system. Lake George, Bangor and Lake Placid remain.

events.title: Lake Placid closes
events.text: The Butler family sells the property to local restaurant owners after nearly 59 years.

events.title: Bangor closes
events.text: The restaurant closes; the motel beside it stays open. One Howard Johnson’s restaurant is left.

events.title: Lake George closes
events.text: The last restaurant shuts and the property is offered for lease. The exact last day of service is not reported.
